## Descriptive statistics

:::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
library(tidyverse)

df |>
  summarise(
    n = sum(!is.na(value)),
    missing = sum(is.na(value)),
    mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    minimum = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(value, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

### Python

```python
import pandas as pd

df["value"].describe(percentiles=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
df["value"].isna().sum()

summary = df.groupby("region")["value"].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "median", "std", "min", "max"]
)
```

## Distributions

:::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
ggplot(df, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(df, aes(region, value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Python

```python
ax = df["value"].plot.hist(bins=30)
ax.set(xlabel="Value")

df.boxplot(column="value", by="region", vert=False)
```
::::

## Cross-tabs and shares

:::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
cross_tab <- janitor::tabyl(df, region, status)
row_shares <- janitor::adorn_percentages(cross_tab, "row")
```

### Python

```python
cross_tab = pd.crosstab(df["region"], df["status"], dropna=False)
row_shares = pd.crosstab(
    df["region"], df["status"], normalize="index", dropna=False
)
```
::::

## Correlations

Correlation describes association, not causation. Inspect missingness and the distributions before interpreting it.

:::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
correlations <- df |>
  select(population, income, turnout) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson")

rank_correlations <- df |>
  select(population, income, turnout) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
```

### Python

```python
columns = ["population", "income", "turnout"]
correlations = df[columns].corr(method="pearson")
rank_correlations = df[columns].corr(method="spearman")
```
::::

## Bins and classifications

:::: {.panel-tabset}
### R

```r
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    fixed_band = cut(
      value,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 10, 25, 50, Inf),
      right = FALSE
    ),
    quintile = ntile(value, 5)
  )
```

### Python

```python
df["fixed_band"] = pd.cut(
    df["value"],
    bins=[float("-inf"), 0, 10, 25, 50, float("inf")],
    right=False,
)
df["quintile"] = pd.qcut(df["value"], q=5, labels=False, duplicates="drop") + 1
```
::::

Quantile classes can contain fewer groups when many observations share boundary values. Fixed thresholds are easier to compare across years; quantiles emphasize relative position within each distribution.

## Tests and regression

Use the language's established statistical functions when a reporting question requires inference; keep model assumptions and diagnostics in the analysis rather than creating a toolbox-wide modeling wrapper.
